summary: Electrical post-fabrication tuning of Al-AlO$_x$-Al Josephson junctions using room-temperature voltage pulses can increase junction resistance up to 270% with a stepped manipulation protocol, enabling transmon qubit frequency shifts of nearly 2 GHz while maintaining quality factors above 1 million. The rate of resistance increase scales exponentially with pulse amplitude ($V_0 = 55$–91 mV depending on oxide dose), and post-manipulation relaxation exhibits both fixed and manipulation-dependent contributions that follow logarithmic time dependence, halting at cryogenic temperatures and resuming at room temperature.
motivation: Superconducting quantum processors suffer from fabrication-induced junction resistance variations (~2% across a 50 mm wafer, corresponding to ±50 MHz frequency spread), causing frequency crowding that severely limits collision-free operations even for ~30 qubits, motivating selective post-fabrication tuning to reach required frequency placement tolerances of a few MHz for 1000-qubit systems.
method: Room-temperature electrical tuning was performed on Al-AlO$_x$-Al junctions from three wafers with different oxidation doses using bipolar voltage pulse trains ($V_a = 0.85$ V, $M = 6$ pulses per iteration, 200 ms duration), with stepped manipulation repeating the process after 3 h relaxation intervals until target resistance or junction failure; qubit decoherence metrics ($T_1$, $T_2^*$, $T_2^e$) were measured on transmon qubits before and after manipulation.
result: Single manipulation cycles achieve 96% resistance increase in 5 min with step-wise relaxation reaching 270% total ($\Delta f \approx -1964$ MHz); relaxation follows $\rho_\mathrm{Total}(t=30\,\mathrm{min}) = k\rho_\mathrm{Active} + m$ with $k = 1.00$–1.13 and manipulation-dependent contributions of ~25% of active resistance change; achieved frequency precision bounded by relaxation offset uncertainty of ±0.19% (~11.3 MHz); transmon quality factors remain $Q = 1$–1.5 million after single-round tuning across high-dose variants.
